One of the fastest ways to trigger a React hydration mismatch in a Next.js App Router application is a single line of date formatting code.

Everything looks completely normal on your local machine. Then you deploy to production, and the browser console throws a hydration error while dates briefly flicker on mobile screens.

Here is why it happens:
Your Next.js Server Component renders the HTML on a Vercel server running in UTC time. When the user opens the page in Jakarta, Sydney, or London, their browser runs client-side hydration using their local timezone and locale settings.

If your component calls new Date().toLocaleDateString() directly during render, the server output and the browser output do not match. React rejects the mismatch and forces an expensive client re-render.

Here are three clean ways we eliminate timezone hydration bugs in production:

1. Lock the Timezone Explicitly on Both Sides:
Never rely on implicit default locales inside Intl.DateTimeFormat or toLocaleDateString. Pass both the locale and an explicit timeZone parameter (for example, 'en-US' and 'UTC' or a stored user timezone preference from the database) so the server and browser produce the exact same string.

2. Defer Local User Timezone Formatting Until Mount:
If you genuinely need the visitor's local browser clock (like "2 hours ago" or local event times), render a deterministic fallback or ISO date on the server, then update to the local string inside a small isolated client wrapper after mount. Never wrap an entire page in a mounted check just to format a timestamp.

3. Pass Serialized ISO Strings Across Server-Client Boundaries:
Pass plain ISO strings from Server Components into Client Components instead of raw Date instances or pre-formatted strings that drop timezone offsets.

Hydration bugs rarely come from complicated business logic. Nine times out of ten, they come from small assumptions about browser globals like window, Date, or invalid nested HTML tags.

Closing the Cloud Loophole: The U.S. Tightens Control Over Global AI Infrastructure
Physical borders no longer define where computing power lives—and U.S. regulators are adjusting their playbook accordingly.
The U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has introduced sweeping new rules aimed at stopping Chinese companies from remotely accessing advanced American AI chips—such as Nvidia’s top-tier processors—through overseas data centers.
Until now, export controls largely focused on blocking the physical shipment of advanced semiconductors into restricted regions. However, cloud computing created an obvious workaround: companies unable to import high-end hardware could simply rent massive computing capacity hosted in third-party countries to train frontier AI models.
What is changing?
 * Tighter Licensing in Key Hubs: Exporting advanced AI chips to major data center hubs—specifically Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil—now requires special U.S. export licenses to prevent diversion.
 * Strict Due Diligence on Cloud Customers: Overseas data center operators using U.S.-designed hardware must verify the ultimate ownership and control of their clients. If a facility provides substantial computing power to companies linked to restricted nations, it faces strict licensing requirements or operational limits.
 * Targeting Indirect Workloads: The regulations look beyond direct contracts, accounting for linked data centers and third-party intermediaries training AI models on behalf of restricted entities.
Why this matters for the tech ecosystem:
For cloud providers and data center operators across Southeast Asia and Latin America, compliance just became a primary competitive differentiator. Infrastructure projects built around international AI demand must now navigate rigorous Know-Your-Customer (KYC) protocols to maintain access to American silicon.
Meanwhile, for AI developers globally, the message is clear: geopolitics isn't just shaping semiconductor supply chains anymore—it is actively redrawing the map of global cloud computing.
How do you see these new cloud restrictions impacting data center investments across emerging tech hubs?

The largest voluntary biodiversity credit transaction in history happened in October.

CDC Biodiversité sold $1m worth of credits from its Tourbières Tuile Pradeaux site, 13% of everything this market has sold since 2022. A milestone for France Crédits Biodiversité and for the market.

We asked CDC for the buyer's identification and data, but have not yet received any. Apparently nothing can be shared until communication is agreed between them, which will take at least another month.

This opacity makes us question the overall market's relation to data sharing. By value, 63% of all corporate purchases ever made are anonymous. Most developers publish a price and a volume, and stop there. After four years and more than $8m of sales, the market still has no common approach to transparency.

Without buyer data, potential buyers cannot see that their peers are moving on credits, investors cannot size the demand, developers cannot target their outreach, and the people designing national schemes work from isolated cases. Each anonymous transaction removes data that everyone in the market could benefit from.

In our experience, this market moves forward through trust, and transparency is one of the best ways to build it. Even when a buyer prefers to stay anonymous, for reasons we understand, there is a lot of value in sharing its sector, size, country and reason for buying. The commercial sensitivity is much lower, and it is exactly what the market is missing.

This is the main story in this month's Monthly Market Overview, alongside twenty governments launching the Friends of Credits for Nature and Biodiversity at COP17, Indonesia saying it wants its market to be mandatory, ten countries moving up our Countries ladder in one month, Cercarbono launching its Nature Integrity Methodology at COP31, and the IAPB's new way to price a credit against direct investment.

📢 WE ARE HIRING: Senior Penetration Tester
 
 
Hello Job Seekers!

I’m Muhammad Hafizh, Tech Recruiter from PT. MSBU Konsultan Indonesia. We are currently looking for one person to join as a Senior Penetration Tester of our client companies for Information Technology Sector Industry in Location DKI Jakarta Area and 12 month Employment Contract.
 
Job Description:
-   Lead technical scoping, establish Rules of Engagement (RoE) with stakeholder and execute end-to-end assessment independently
-   Perform deep dive assessment on Web, Mobile (Android/iOS), API (REST/GraphQL), Network, Active Directory, and Cloud/Container environments with manual validation to eliminate false positives
-   Produce clear, two-tiered report consisting of an Executive Summary for leadership and reproducible technical details with prioritized remediation steps for developer
-   Lead debrief session, presenting complex technical finding effectively to both non-technical business leader and technical engineering team
-   Conduct retest to verify fix effectiveness and ensure long-term risk mitigation
-   Drive continuous improvement by building internal tooling, refining checklist/playbook and mentoring junior team member
 
 
Requirement:
-   Minimum 4 years of experience in offensive security or 7 years in general cybersecurity with at least 4 years exclusively focus on penetration testing, experience bug bounty.
-   Proven experience independently managing critical engagement within high-risk sector (Financial Services, Telecommunication, E-Commerce or Government)
-   In-depth knowledge of OWASP Top 10 and WSTG. Expertise in testing authentication/authorization flaws, IDOR, SSRF, insecure deserialization, business logic bugs, and API vulnerabilities (REST & GraphQL batching/introspection abuse)
-  Deep knowledge of OWASP MASTG, Hands on experience with static/dynamic analysis on Android & iOS, including client-side security bypasses
-  Proficient in Python, Bash or PowerShell (Go or C# is a plus).
-  Familiar with PTES, OSSTMM, NIST SP 800-115, MITRE ATT&CK, CVSS v3.1/v4.0, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, as well as Indonesian regulation (POJK/SEOJK and UU PDP)
-  Preferred Certification (Practical/Hands-on): OSCP (Primary), paired with OSEP, OSWE, GPEN, GWAPT, CRTO or CREST CRT
-  Bonus / Advanced: OSCE³, GXPN, CARTP/CARTS, eWPTX, or GMOB
-  Complementary: CEH, CompTIA PenTest+

Great design only becomes reality when every stakeholder sees the exact same vision.

​When Indonesian multidisciplinary design firm Arkonin took on civic landmarks like Jakarta’s Pinisi Crossing Bridge, aligning engineers, urban planners, and decision-makers around the vision was critical. 

"SketchUp was pivotal in enabling our architects to visualize material interactions, particularly between concrete and steel. The team leveraged the software's dynamic 3D modeling and scene creation tools to illustrate how the new bridge would evolve from its existing structure."

By building a shared 3D foundation in Trimble SketchUp—the firm brought their vision to life with SketchUp.

​AECO teams can now use SketchUp from initial concept to project execution:

→ Align stakeholders: Anchor architecture, engineering, and landscape scopes around one clear base model.
→ De-risk complex sites: Test massing, walkability, and topography before committing to detailed documentation.
→ Accelerate client buy-in: Convey how the final design will look like
